blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Managing delivery SLAs and time windows in practice is a balancing act. Customers want the tightest possible windows; operations can only keep the ones they are actually built to hit. A gap between these two — promises that look good on the website but cannot be held on a real Tuesday — is the single biggest source of customer complaints in most logistics businesses.

The fix is honesty. If you cannot reliably hold a two-hour window across the whole city, do not promise one. Promise a three-hour window you can hit ninety-five per cent of the time. Customers, it turns out, prefer reliable honesty to heroic optimism.

Good SLA design also includes what happens when something goes wrong. If we miss the window, will we warn the customer early? Will we offer a refund? Will we try again the next day? A clear answer, known in advance, turns a failure into a mildly annoying event instead of a crisis.

items.q: According to the text, what is the single biggest source of customer complaints?
options: Refund policies that are too generous
The gap between promised windows and what operations can hold
Websites that are hard to use
items.why: "A gap between these two… is the single biggest source of customer complaints."

items.q: What does the author recommend if you cannot reliably hold a two-hour window?
options: Promise a two-hour window anyway and apologise later
Promise a three-hour window you can hit 95% of the time
Let customers choose their own window
Stop offering deliveries in that area
items.why: "Promise a three-hour window you can hit ninety-five per cent of the time."

items.q: What makes a missed delivery "a mildly annoying event instead of a crisis"?
options: A clear recovery plan known in advance
items.why: "A clear answer, known in advance, turns a failure into a mildly annoying event."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: You should plan for what happens when a delivery fails.
Advertising the tightest possible window always wins more customers.
Reliability matters more than an impressive-looking promise.
Honesty reduces complaints in the long run.
items.why: Inferência: o texto argumenta que promessas otimistas que não se cumprem geram reclamações — 'reliable honesty over heroic optimism'.

items.q: The phrase "heroic optimism" suggests that the author sees ambitious promises as…
options: the only way to compete on price
items.why: Inferência: 'heroic' aqui é irônico — soa bonito, mas não se sustenta, ao contrário da 'reliable honesty'.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Sophie explicar a nova política de janelas de entrega. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Okay, so I've spent the last two weeks with the operations data, and the picture is clear. The website has been promising two-hour windows citywide, but honestly, we only hit that in one neighbourhood out of six. Everywhere else, we are late roughly a third of the time.

Here is what I'm proposing. From next month, the standard window becomes three hours, not two. It's less impressive on the page, I know, but our own numbers say we can hold it about ninety-five per cent of the time. If we can hit that reliably, customers will trust the badge — and trust is what actually keeps them.

The second half is just as important. Right now, when we miss a slot, nobody tells the customer until the driver simply doesn't show. That has to stop. If a delivery is going to run late, the system will send a text the moment we know, and we'll offer either a redelivery the next morning or a small credit.

I'd rather promise a little less and keep every word of it. If we do that consistently, the complaints will fall — and the ones we do get will be about the weather, not about us.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: How many neighbourhoods did the two-hour window actually work in?
items.why: "we only hit that in one neighbourhood out of six."

items.q: What change to the standard window is Sophie proposing?
options: Moving from two hours to three hours
Moving from three hours to two hours
items.why: "From next month, the standard window becomes three hours, not two."

items.q: What will happen when a delivery is going to run late?
options: The driver will simply not show up
The customer will be charged a rescheduling fee
Nothing changes until the customer complains
The system will send a text and offer a redelivery or a credit
items.why: "the system will send a text… and we'll offer either a redelivery the next morning or a small credit."

items.q: What does Sophie mean by "the ones we do get will be about the weather, not about us"?
options: Customers will start complaining about the app design
The company will blame the weather for every failure
Remaining complaints will be about things outside the company's control
items.why: Inferência: se a operação cumpre a promessa, sobram só causas externas (clima), não falhas próprias.

items.q: What is Sophie's underlying priority in this proposal?
options: Cutting delivery costs as fast as possible
Making the website look as impressive as possible
Winning customers on the tightest window available
Building trust by promising less and keeping every word
items.why: Inferência: "I'd rather promise a little less and keep every word of it" — a prioridade é confiança, não a vitrine.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Setting delivery targets is a balancing act between speed and reliability." A balancing act is…
options: a situation requiring a careful trade-off between competing needs
items.why: Balancing act = ato de equilíbrio: gerir necessidades que puxam em direções opostas.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "There was a ___ between what the website promised and what we could actually deliver."
items.why: Gap = lacuna: a diferença entre a promessa e a realidade.

items.q: "We now offer a three-hour delivery window." Here, a window is…
options: a period of time in which something is expected to happen
an opening in the warehouse wall
items.why: Window = janela (de tempo): o intervalo em que a entrega deve ocorrer.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "A ___ service keeps its promise almost every time, so customers stop checking."
items.why: Reliable = confiável: cumpre o que promete de forma consistente.

items.q: "When a slot is at risk, we warn the customer immediately." To warn someone means to…
options: tell them in advance about a problem
items.why: To warn = avisar: comunicar com antecedência que algo pode dar errado.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em reuniões sobre entregas e nível de serviço. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "Operations still has to sign off on the new three-hour window." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We'll roll out the new SLA region by region." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva.

items.q: "Two team leads pushed back on the tighter window." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "The team agreed to send early alerts but never followed through." They…
options: carried the plan out to the end
failed to actually do what they agreed
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado; aqui, não fizeram.

items.q: "Shaving ten minutes off the window won't move the needle on complaints." This means it will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.
